rows: 4.1 BASIS OF CLASSIFICATION

Inspite of differences in structure and form of different animals, there are fundamental features common to various individuals in relation to the arrangement of cells, body symmetry, nature of coelom, patterns of digestive, circulatory or reproductive systems.
structure form animals arrangement cells body symmetry coelom digestive circulatory reproductive systems basis classification
4.1.1 Levels of Organisation
Though all members of Animalia are multicellular, all of them do not exhibit the same pattern of organisation of cells.
animalia multicellular organisation cells sponges cellular level
4.1.2 Symmetry
Animals can be categorised on the basis of their symmetry.
animals symmetry sponges asymmetrical plane equal halves
4.1.3 Diploblastic and Triploblastic Organisation
Animals in which cells are arranged in two embryonic layers are called diploblastic animals.
diploblastic triploblastic ectoderm endoderm mesoglea embryonic layers
4.1.4 Coelom
The body cavity lined by mesoderm is called coelom.
coelom body cavity mesoderm gut wall classification
4.1.5 Segmentation
In some animals the body is divided into segments with serial repetition of organs.
segmentation metameric metamerism earthworm segments organs
4.1.6 Notochord
Notochord is a mesodermally derived rod-like structure formed on the dorsal side during embryonic development.
notochord mesoderm dorsal embryonic chordates non-chordates
4.2 CLASSIFICATION OF ANIMALS
Animalia is broadly classified using common fundamental features.
classification animals animalia fundamental features
4.2.1 Phylum – Porifera
Members of Porifera are commonly known as sponges.
porifera sponges marine asymmetrical
4.2.2 Phylum – Coelenterata (Cnidaria)
Cnidarians are aquatic, mostly marine, sessile or free-swimming, radially symmetrical animals.
coelenterata cnidaria aquatic marine sessile free-swimming radial symmetry
4.2.3 Phylum – Ctenophora
Ctenophores are sea walnuts or comb jellies and are exclusively marine.
ctenophora ctenophores sea walnuts comb jellies marine radial diploblastic ciliated comb plates
4.2.4 Phylum – Platyhelminthes
Platyhelminthes have dorso-ventrally flattened bodies and are called flatworms.
platyhelminthes flatworms endoparasites human
4.2.5 Phylum – Aschelminthes
Aschelminthes are circular in cross-section and are called roundworms.
aschelminthes roundworms aquatic terrestrial parasitic plants animals
4.2.6 Phylum – Annelida
Annelids may be aquatic or terrestrial, free-living or sometimes parasitic.
annelida aquatic marine freshwater terrestrial parasitic organ-system bilateral symmetry
4.2.7 Phylum – Arthropoda
Arthropoda is the largest phylum of Animalia and includes insects.
arthropoda largest phylum animalia insects arthropods
4.2.8 Phylum – Mollusca
Mollusca is the second largest animal phylum.
mollusca molluscs terrestrial aquatic marine freshwater organ-system
4.2.9 Phylum – Echinodermata
Echinoderms have an endoskeleton of calcareous ossicles.
echinodermata spiny bodied endoskeleton calcareous ossicles marine
4.2.10 Phylum – Hemichordata
Hemichordata is placed as a separate phylum under non-chordata.
hemichordata chordata non-chordata phylum
4.2.11 Phylum – Chordata
Chordates are fundamentally characterised by the presence of a notochord.
chordata chordates notochord dorsal
5.1 THE ROOT
In most dicotyledonous plants, elongation of the radicle forms the primary root.
root dicotyledonous radicle primary lateral secondary tertiary
5.1.1 Regions of the Root
The root apex is covered by a root cap.
root cap apex soil regions
5.2 THE STEM
The stem is the ascending part of the axis bearing branches, leaves, flowers and fruits.
stem axis branches leaves flowers fruits
5.3 THE LEAF
The leaf is a lateral, generally flattened structure borne on the stem.
leaf lateral flattened stem node bud axil
5.3.1 Venation
The arrangement of veins and veinlets in the lamina is termed venation.
venation veins veinlets lamina reticulate
5.3.2 Types of Leaves
Leaves may be simple or compound depending on incisions of the lamina.
simple compound leaf lamina midrib leaflets
5.3.3 Phyllotaxy
Phyllotaxy is the pattern of arrangement of leaves on the stem or branch.
phyllotaxy alternate opposite whorled leaves stem branch
5.4 THE INFLORESCENCE
A flower is a modified shoot in which the shoot apical meristem changes to floral meristem.
inflorescence flower modified shoot apical meristem floral internodes axis
5.5 THE FLOWER
The flower is the reproductive unit in angiosperms.
flower reproductive unit angiosperms sexual reproduction
5.5.1 Parts of a Flower
A typical flower has calyx, corolla, androecium and gynoecium.
flower floral whorls calyx corolla androecium gynoecium
5.6 THE FRUIT
Fruit is a mature or ripened ovary developed after fertilisation.
fruit flowering plants ovary fertilisation
5.7 THE SEED
Ovules after fertilisation develop into seeds.
seed ovules fertilisation seed coat embryo
5.7.1 Structure of a Dicotyledonous Seed
A seed coat has an outer testa and inner tegmen.
dicotyledonous seed coat testa tegmen
5.7.2 Structure of Monocotyledonous Seed
Most monocotyledonous seeds are endospermic.
monocotyledonous seeds endospermic orchids non-endospermic cereals maize
5.8 SEMI-TECHNICAL DESCRIPTION OF A TYPICAL FLOWERING PLANT
Morphological features are used to describe a flowering plant in scientific sequence.
morphological features flowering plant description scientific language
5.9 SOLANACEAE
Solanaceae is a large family commonly called the potato family.
solanaceae potato family tropics subtropics temperate
6.1 THE TISSUE SYSTEM
Plant tissues vary depending on their location in the plant body.
tissue system plant tissues cells location
6.1.1 Epidermal Tissue System
The epidermal tissue system forms the outermost covering of the plant body.
epidermal tissue epidermis stomata appendages trichomes hairs
6.1.2 The Ground Tissue System
All tissues except epidermis and vascular bundles constitute ground tissue.
ground tissue epidermis vascular bundles parenchyma collenchyma sclerenchyma
6.1.3 The Vascular Tissue System
The vascular system consists of phloem and xylem.
vascular tissue phloem xylem bundles cambium dicotyledonous stems
6.2 ANATOMY OF DICOTYLEDONOUS AND MONOCOTYLEDONOUS PLANTS
Roots, stems and leaves can be studied in transverse section to understand tissue organisation.
anatomy dicotyledonous monocotyledonous roots stems leaves transverse sections tissue organisation
6.2.1 Dicotyledonous Root
The sunflower root transverse section shows an outermost epiblema.
dicotyledonous root sunflower transverse section epiblema
6.2.2 Monocotyledonous Root
Monocot root has epidermis, cortex, endodermis, pericycle, vascular bundles and pith.
monocotyledonous root epidermis cortex endodermis pericycle vascular bundles pith
6.2.3 Dicotyledonous Stem
A young dicotyledonous stem has an outermost protective epidermis.
dicotyledonous stem transverse section epidermis protective layer
6.2.4 Monocotyledonous Stem
Monocot stem has sclerenchymatous hypodermis and scattered vascular bundles.
monocotyledonous stem sclerenchymatous hypodermis vascular bundles bundle sheath parenchymatous ground tissue conjoint closed
6.2.5 Dorsiventral (Dicotyledonous) Leaf
A dorsiventral leaf has epidermis, mesophyll and vascular system.
dorsiventral dicotyledonous leaf epidermis mesophyll vascular system adaxial abaxial
6.2.6 Isobilateral (Monocotyledonous) Leaf
Isobilateral leaf anatomy resembles dorsiventral leaf anatomy with characteristic differences.
isobilateral monocotyledonous leaf dorsiventral anatomy
